questions: Where does almost all the mass of an atom sit?
What fills the space between the nucleus and the outer shell?
segments.say: Inside the atom. Watch the three shells draw themselves first, then the nucleus growing at the centre, then the electrons dropping into their shells. Notice how much of the picture is just empty space - almost all the mass sits in that tiny nucleus. Tell your partner: where is the mass, and what fills the rest of the atom?

questions: How many protons and electrons does a carbon atom have?
segments.say: Counting particles: carbon. Carbon is element 6: count the six protons in the nucleus, then watch its six electrons fill the shells two, then four. We write that arrangement as 2,4. Say it with me: the proton number fixes the element.

questions: How do you work out sodium's 12 neutrons?
Why does the single outer electron matter so much?
segments.say: Counting particles: sodium. Sodium is element 11: eleven protons, twelve neutrons - that is nucleon number 23 minus proton number 11 - and eleven electrons. Watch the shells fill two, eight, then one lonely electron in shell 3. That lone outer electron rules sodium's chemistry.

questions: What do all elements in one group share?
Why does that make their reactions similar?
segments.say: Groups: the table's columns. Trace one column with me: every element in it has the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways - a family resemblance written in electrons. Now check the worksheet question on sodium and potassium.

questions: What does the period number count?
How many shells does a period 2 element have?
segments.say: Periods: the table's rows. Follow a row across: each period starts a new outer shell, so the period number simply counts the shells - period 2 has two shells, period 3 has three. Quick check with your partner: how many shells does a period 3 element have?

questions: Which picture of the atom will you use from now on, and why?
What would you say to someone who draws an atom as a solid ball?
segments.say: A common mistake, sprung on purpose. Watch the solid marble picture, then watch it give way to the shell model: a speck of a nucleus in mostly empty space, electrons in fixed shells - not planets circling. Now work through the worksheet in pairs, checking each answer against the trap section of your student notes. Last, the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - and remember: count the particles, then let the shells tell you the group and period.
segments.watchFor: Atoms are solid balls. Listen for students who draw or describe a solid marble atom. Send them back to the shell model: Atoms are mostly empty space: the electrons sit far from a tiny dense nucleus.
